cells.tense: You are noticing what arrives and giving it words that land in the room.
cells.ask: Take one thing that's arriving this week, put it into plain words for someone who hasn't asked, and stay while they take it in.
cells.core:
You catch what's coming before it fully lands and you can turn it into something other people can hold. That's the plain skill here: naming the meaningful thing so it travels. Noticed early, said without a pitch, left open for someone else to take or leave. It shows in the weekly meeting where you say the sentence colleagues were circling, and in the conversation where a friend leaves with words they didn't have before.

It's steady right now. You walk toward what connects instead of waiting to be found, and saying it keeps its weight without turning into a sales job. The bend would be chasing the connection so hard you miss the moment it was ready — you're not doing that today. What this balance is free to feed next is someone else's arrival, not your own. The thing that walked in this week hasn't been handed to anyone yet. Hand it over before the moment cools.
cells.sheetLine: You catch what arrives and give it words that carry.
cells.verb: Naming what matters into words that carry
cells.place: Where what's arriving first comes through you

cells.tense: You are pulling the next moment into this one before it has shown up on its own.
cells.ask: Ask one person for something small they can actually give this week, and don't answer it or fill the silence after.
cells.core:
You're running one beat ahead of the room. Something's coming, and you're already three exchanges past it, bracing for a version that hasn't arrived. The pushing feels like care. It lands as pressure, and you can hear it in your own voice when you replay the conversation.

You're charging at the connection before it opens. Forcing it now doesn't get the person closer — it gets a version of them that agreed too fast, and that hollowness follows you home. That's the cost. Let the arrival take its own tempo instead. Not softer, just one step slower. The moment you're bracing for may not be the moment that actually comes, and you'd hate to have spent the week fighting a guest who didn't show.

cells.tense: You are standing at the last arrival point and the new one is coming in behind you.
cells.ask: Write down one thing worth keeping from the last arrival, in plain sentences, and put it where you'll see it next week.
cells.core:
Something came and went, and you're still turned toward where it entered. The new thing is arriving, real and already here, and you're not meeting it. When this works, you notice what's come in and you say it — to a friend, in a note, out loud to yourself — and the saying is what lets you move on. You did that before. You can still do it.

That's why nothing lands now. You're waiting at the wrong opening for a guest who already walked through. Put the last arrival into words. Not for anyone else yet, just so you and the meaning sit in the same place. Then turn around. The next thing hasn't been given words, and you're the one who gives them.

cells.tense: You are already deciding what the arrival means and calling it the shape of things.
cells.ask: Say out loud the one judgment you've already made about what's arriving, and own it as your call rather than as how things are.
cells.core:
You already read what comes in. You sort which part matters, what it points to, what it means for you next — and you do it well enough that you talk about the meaning as if it arrived wearing its own name. Done right, that reading is yours and carries your own mark, and you can hand it to someone as a judgment you stand behind.

It hasn't been claimed. Say one of those judgments as yours. Not to be right about it, just to stop handing the deciding to the moment itself. You set the temperature in here, and it would help to know that when the next thing arrives.
